name: Thunderbird
title: Thunderbird Review: A Free Email Client, Compared with MailVault
description: Thunderbird vs MailVault: compare free desktop email, offline access, profile backups, portable archives, and everyday usability.
intro: Thunderbird belongs on a shortlist of desktop email clients because it gives you room to build your own workflow. The question is whether you want a configurable email workspace or a client that makes keeping your email a central part of the experience. For the second job, MailVault is our first choice.
strength: Thunderbird combines email, calendars, and contacts on Windows, macOS, and Linux. It is free, open source, and supports separate accounts or a unified inbox. Its flexibility is a good fit if you enjoy choosing how your mail is organized instead of accepting a fixed workflow.
scenario: Picture a household with several personal addresses and a club mailbox. A customizable client can bring those accounts into one place while preserving their identities. Before you choose, try your actual folders, reply from each address, and check whether the layout still makes sense when all accounts are busy. A long feature list matters less than reliably answering from the right account.
limitTitle: Offline synchronization needs a separate backup decision
limit: Thunderbird can download messages for offline use, but IMAP synchronization also reflects deletions from the server. Keeping an offline copy in a synchronized account is therefore different from maintaining an independent backup. Mozilla explains both the synchronization behavior and the need to download message bodies for full-text search.
archive: Thunderbird does have a real backup route: its Export tool saves accounts, messages, address books, and settings in a profile ZIP. Mozilla documents a 2 GB ZIP limit and a manual profile-copy method for larger profiles. That is useful when moving a whole installation, though it asks you to think in terms of profiles rather than individual saved messages.
platform: Windows, macOS, Linux; Android app available
archivePath: Profile ZIP export or manual profile copy
aiPath: Customization is the focus of this review
graphic: Export a profile to back it up
mailvaultCaption: MailVault’s custody indicators distinguish messages on the server, in the vault, or in both places. Demo data from the supplied product tour.
mailvault: MailVault makes the location of each message visible. You can read and reply in the same app, archive messages as portable .eml files, and search saved mail locally. That is a more direct fit for someone who wants to know whether a receipt is safely kept before removing its server copy. The free app includes manual backups; Premium adds scheduled backups and Time Capsule snapshots.
verdict: MailVault is our winner. Thunderbird offers extensive customization and profile backups. MailVault wins our local-ownership comparison by making message custody visible and keeping portable .eml originals, local search, and manual backups inside the everyday email workflow. For readers who want to read, keep, and find their own email, MailVault is our recommendation.

name: Microsoft Outlook
title: Outlook Review: Microsoft 365 Convenience vs MailVault’s Local Ownership
description: Outlook vs MailVault: compare Microsoft 365 workflows, desktop export, offline mail, pricing models, and local email ownership.
intro: Outlook is an obvious candidate when your working day already revolves around Microsoft 365. But the best client for a workplace calendar is not automatically the best place to keep a personal email archive. MailVault is our first choice when direct access to locally saved messages is the deciding factor.
strengthTitle: A good fit for a Microsoft-centered workday
strength: Microsoft presents Outlook as a place for email, calendars, and contacts across desktop, mobile, and web. It supports personal, work, and school accounts, with connections to services such as Gmail and iCloud. Its appeal is the ability to handle correspondence and scheduling in a familiar Microsoft environment.
scenario: For an employee whose invitations, shared workflows, and support desk are built around Microsoft, compatibility can outweigh personal preferences. Start there: test a meeting invitation and your normal account permissions. If the organization supplies Outlook, you may already have the right daily tool. The remaining question is how you keep the messages you are permitted to retain when the account or job changes.
limitTitle: The Outlook version changes the export workflow
limit: Microsoft’s current guidance includes PST export in new Outlook for Windows through Settings → Files → Export. The same guidance says importing a mailbox or calendar from PST into a mailbox still requires classic Outlook, and calendar/contact items in PST are unavailable in new Outlook. Check the exact version before building a recovery plan around it.
archive: Microsoft also tells classic Outlook users to download all the mail they intend to export; the default download period may omit older messages. A successful export dialog is not sufficient proof that the archive contains your entire history. Open representative messages from several years and inspect their attachments before relying on the file.
price: Free Outlook options exist; classic desktop apps and additional features depend on the Microsoft 365 or Office license.
platform: Desktop, web, and mobile; features vary by version
archivePath: PST export on supported Windows versions
aiPath: Copilot eligibility depends on account and plan
mailvaultCaption: MailVault’s local search combines sender and keyword filters across saved mail. The displayed timing belongs to this demo capture, not a benchmark against Outlook.
mailvault: MailVault puts your saved messages on your own disk as .eml files and builds a local search index. You can use it for reading and replying as well as keeping a durable copy of important correspondence. For an independent archive, that gives you a straightforward path from a search result to the original message without designing your workflow around a PST container. For workplace accounts, verify the connection your organization permits.
verdict: MailVault is our winner. Outlook offers strong Microsoft 365 scheduling and workplace integration. MailVault wins our local-ownership comparison with directly accessible .eml originals and local archive search, giving personal email retention a clear workflow beyond version-specific PST export. For readers who want to read, keep, and find their own email, MailVault is our recommendation.

archive: An export is only useful if the mailbox contains what you intended to preserve. For your own check, choose one old conversation, one attachment, and one sent message, then confirm they are present in the exported archive. Keep a second copy on another drive. A local archive still depends on the health of the computer and disk holding it.

platform: Apple devices; this review focuses on macOS
aiPath: Apple Intelligence Writing Tools on supported setups

MailVault also offers AI writing and thread summaries using a supported on-device model, alongside the underlying original mail.
verdict: MailVault is our winner. Apple Mail offers a familiar built-in experience and mailbox exports. MailVault wins our local-ownership comparison by combining visible message custody, individual .eml originals, local archive search, and the same desktop app across macOS, Windows, and Linux.
